stories.title: Mountain of broken fridges growing across England and Wales
stories.summary: A mountain of broken fridges is building up in waste centres across England and Wales, the Local Government Association (LGA) has warned. This year's multiple heat waves have increased the numbers of white goods such as fridges and freezers breaking down and needing to be scrapped at specialist sites. Dozens of councils have been forced to stop collections of white goods due to a major backlog, which has built up due to a national shortage of specialists needed to safely process the appliances. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced the latest crackdown on illegal waste dumps - and the LGA is now calling on the government to take urgent action on dealing with white goods too. LGA Neighbourhoods committee chair Councillor Arooj Shah called on the government to force white goods companies to pick up the burden, help councils with the cost of extra storage, and prevent the same problems recurring in future. "The backlog of defunct white goods is getting bigger by the day – they're at risk of becoming a mountain," he said. "It is not right that residents who are trying to do the right thing can't take old or broken appliances to their local recycling centre due to failures elsewhere in the system." Councils from Bradford to Gloucestershire, Durham and Nottingham are among 26 to have suspended fridge collections this month. A Department for Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) spokesman acknowledged the capacity issues and said short-term storage was being set up. He said: "Our priority is to minimise disruption to household collection or proper disposal of fridges and other cooling equipment, and we are pushing producers of these items to take all necessary steps to achieve this and resolve any collection delays." Fridges and freezers require specialist dismantling due to the gases they contain, which can be harmful to the environment if not disposed of safely, but three of the UK's 10 full-scale processing plants have closed in the last 12 months. The three closures - due to a fire, bankruptcy and a change of use - have been compounded by this year's heat waves, as the remaining plants cannot operate above 30 degrees Celsius.

stories.title: US revises statements suggesting Chinese hackers attacked agencies
stories.summary: The US Department of Justice clarifies that the US Senate and Federal Reserve were targets but were not successfully hacked. United States officials have corrected earlier statements that several government agencies were attacked by Chinese hackers, now saying instead that the organisations were only among the hackers’ targets. A previous version of the statement said the government agencies had been among the hackers’ victims. A note at the bottom of the newly revised statement says: “Edits have been made to ensure this press release accurately reflects the government’s allegations in the affidavit in support of the domain seizures.” The Justice Department said on Friday it made a correction to the news release because the August 26 release “described all agencies as victims whereas the government’s affidavit made clear that all were targeted but only some were compromised”. The distinction matters because it narrows the scope of confirmed breaches. The Justice Department has accused Chinese actors of a years-long cyber-espionage campaign against US government agencies, defence contractors and other sensitive targets. According to an affidavit from the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) released alongside the original statement, the hackers have “targeted” US federal networks since at least 2018. Those targets include NASA, the Federal Reserve, the Department of Energy (DOE), the Department of Justice, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US Senate. A footnote in the affidavit said that the FBI investigated the targeting of NASA and found that the attempted breach of NASA was unsuccessful due to the agency’s patching of targeted software. The affidavit alleges that in September 2024, the hackers carried out “computer intrusions” at three “DOE National Laboratories, NIH, an HHS agency, and a US security device manufacturer”. It referred to the entities as “victims”.

stories.title: Strong winds and thunderstorms kick off the bank holiday weekend
stories.summary: After weeks of scorching heat and drought the summer's swan song is set to be one of frequent downpours as well as gales for some. Areas of heavy rain and showers are expected to sweep across parts of the UK on each day of the weekend, which is a bank holiday for many. This could make for some soggy moments at many of the festivals taking place over the coming days. Strong winds and gales may also cause problems for travellers and holidaymakers in southern parts of the UK. Will it rain everywhere this weekend? Let us start with the good news - for many of us it won't be a complete washout of a weekend. It is certainly worth looking deeper into your weather app forecasts to see the hourly breakdown as showers can sometimes be tricky to forecast. Most areas will still see some drier and sunnier moments through the three days, with parts of north and west Scotland perhaps seeing very little rainfall at all. During the sunnier spells the late August sunshine still has enough strength to make it feels reasonably warm too. However, on Saturday the forecast shows several zones of heavy showers sweeping across England and Wales especially. Like recent days some of these could be torrential and thundery, especially in the southern half of England and Wales. For northern parts of England the showers are likely to merge into longer spells of rain during the afternoon.
